Datasets, experimental results, benchmarks, and reproducibility packages will be incorporated as they are curated. When appropriate, preserved research objects will be linked to persistent repositories and identifiers.

title: Software & Data
text:
Preservation Model
The long-term preservation strategy separates three layers:

Development — source code and active collaboration environments;
Publication — stable releases associated with papers, projects, and academic outputs;
Preservation — durable research objects with persistent metadata and, where appropriate, archival repositories and DOIs.

This structure is intended to preserve relationships such as:
project → software → release → dataset → publication → student → talk

title: Research
text:
My research investigates the foundations, mechanisms and infrastructures required to establish security and trust in digital environments.
It spans a spectrum from cryptographic and mathematical foundations to large-scale digital trust infrastructures, with increasing attention to the challenges introduced by post-quantum cryptography and autonomous artificial-intelligence agents.

title: Research
text:
Research Foundations

Cryptography
My work in cryptography includes cryptographic algorithms and protocols, security mechanisms, key management, digital signatures and the design and analysis of cryptographic systems.
A recurring objective is to connect cryptographic constructions with their practical use in secure computing infrastructures.


Finite-Field Arithmetic
Efficient arithmetic over finite fields is an important component of many cryptographic systems.
My research includes arithmetic over binary extension fields, particularly efficient polynomial multiplication, squaring and modular reduction in \(\mathrm{GF}(2^m)\).
Current work investigates structured families of irreducible polynomials and methods for reducing the computational complexity of finite-field arithmetic.

title: Research
text:
Digital Trust

Digital Signatures
Digital signatures have been one of the central themes of my research.
My work addresses signature mechanisms, signature systems, cryptographic key management, certification, validation and the long-term trustworthiness of digitally signed information.
A particular interest is the complete lifecycle of digital signatures, from identity establishment and key generation to long-term validation and preservation.


Public Key Infrastructure
My research on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) investigates the technologies, protocols and trust models required to establish cryptographic identities and trustworthy digital transactions.
This work includes digital certificates, certification authorities, key management, certificate lifecycle management and the integration of PKI with real-world information systems.


Digital Identity
Digital identity has progressively become a major component of my research.
Topics include authentication, authorization, identity federation, OpenID Connect, OAuth, electronic identity and verifiable credentials.
A central question is how identity attributes and credentials can be represented, verified and used while maintaining security, privacy, interoperability and user control.


Electronic Documents
My research on electronic documents investigates how documents can remain authentic, verifiable and trustworthy throughout their lifecycle.
This includes digital signatures, document formats, validation evidence, trusted timestamps and long-term digital preservation.
The objective is not merely to protect a file, but to preserve the ability to establish the authenticity and integrity of a digital document over long periods of time.

title: Research
Research
text:
Current Research Questions
Several questions currently connect these research areas:

How should autonomous AI agents be identified and authorized when acting on behalf of people or organizations?
How can the actions of autonomous agents produce trustworthy and auditable digital evidence?
How should digital-signature and PKI infrastructures evolve during the transition to post-quantum cryptography?
Which irreducible-polynomial structures lead to more efficient arithmetic over binary finite fields?
How can digital identity evolve from centralized identity providers toward portable and verifiable digital credentials?
How can electronic documents remain verifiable for decades despite changes in cryptographic algorithms, technologies and trust infrastructures?

title: Research
text:
Research Philosophy
Across these topics, my research follows a common principle:

Digital trust requires more than cryptographic algorithms.

It requires the integration of cryptography, identity, protocols, software, governance and long-term evidence into systems that can be deployed and operated in real environments.
This connection between foundations and deployable systems has been a recurring theme throughout my research.

title: About
text:
I am a professor and researcher in computer science, working primarily in information security and cryptography. My research spans digital signatures, public key infrastructure, digital identity, electronic documents, cryptographic protocols, post-quantum cryptography, finite-field arithmetic, and artificial intelligence applied to security.
I am a Full Professor at the Department of Informatics and Statistics of the Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC), in Florianópolis, Brazil, and supervisor of the Computer Security Laboratory (LabSEC).
Throughout my academic career, I have combined fundamental and applied research with the development of technologies and infrastructures for real-world digital trust systems.


I received my Bachelor’s degree in Electrical Engineering from the Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC), followed by a Master’s degree in Electrical Engineering at the same university.
I received my PhD in Computer Science from the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS) in 1999.
I joined UFSC as a faculty member in 1994. Over the following decades, my academic activities have included teaching, research, technology development, graduate supervision, and collaboration with public and private institutions.



My work is centered on the security and trust mechanisms required for digital systems.
My main research interests include:

information security;
cryptography and cryptographic protocols;
digital signatures and electronic signatures;
public key infrastructure (PKI);
digital identity and authentication;
electronic documents and long-term preservation;
cryptographic key management;
arithmetic over finite fields;
post-quantum cryptography;
artificial intelligence applied to security and digital trust.

A recurring theme in my research is the connection between cryptographic foundations and deployable systems: how mathematical, cryptographic and security mechanisms can be transformed into infrastructures and applications that operate in real institutional environments.



I supervise the Computer Security Laboratory (LabSEC) at UFSC.
LabSEC conducts research and technology development in information security and cryptography, bringing together undergraduate, Master’s and PhD students and collaborating with universities, government institutions and organizations involved in digital infrastructures.
Over the years, the laboratory has worked on topics including public key infrastructure, digital certification, digital signatures, electronic documents, digital identity, cryptographic protocols, blockchain technologies and post-quantum cryptography.



An important part of my academic work has been the education and supervision of researchers.
I supervise undergraduate research, Master’s dissertations and PhD theses, particularly in information security, cryptography, digital identity and trustworthy digital infrastructures.
Many of the research projects developed with students combine theoretical investigation with the design, implementation and experimental evaluation of security technologies.
Students and supervision →



My work also involves research, development and innovation projects with institutions outside the university.
These collaborations have provided opportunities to apply research in areas such as digital certification, electronic documents, civil registration, digital identity, financial infrastructures and post-quantum security.
